context: ARBITER computes proposed ratings and permits a reasoned, recorded override with its rationale and evidence. Thus, the software guarantees a checked proposal and an auditable route for any departure; it does not make interpretation infallible. We checked proposed and adopted ratings separately. AVATAR illustrates the workflow for all-cause death after early surgery versus watchful waiting in asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (Figure 2; <supplement>). It was selected to explain the process, rather than represent typical performance. Its stored documents did not establish a dated analysis plan for the assessed result.
intended_captions: AVATAR complete trace

context: The benchmark comprised trials from published meta-analyses, with source reviews, specialties and label distributions documented in <supplement>. Assessment prompts targeted the published review's labelled result using its outcome, time point, contrast and printed result, rather than automatically choosing the trial's primary outcome. The binding audit identified 33 explicit result matches, 11 matches within several covered outcomes, 32 inferred matches, 7 partial matches, 9 different results and 10 unknown bindings. Twelve label sets were trial-wide, seven jointly covered pain and disability, and ten had unknown result binding; these categories were retained rather than relabelled as exact result matches. De Waal's supplied registry record belongs to another trial; its presence does not establish relevant information about the assessed result.

Published label distributions by domain

context: The analysis included 102 trials from 16 meta-analyses, yielding 510 domain cells per arm and 81 trials with published Overall labels (Figure 3; <supplement>). Three unsupported trial designs were excluded from both arms. Adjudicators reviewed 154 disputed domain cells, agreed on a preferred rating in 129 and split in 25. The arms differed in 80 reviewed cells, comprising 62 with an agreed choice and 18 with split decisions.
intended_captions: Benchmark trials span sixteen meta-analyses

context: Both models agreed poorly with published review labels: weighted κ was 0.34 (95% CI 0.26–0.42) for ARBITER and 0.28 (0.21–0.35) for Unassisted (Table 1; Figure 4A). Exact agreement was 386/510 (75.7%) and 395/510 (77.5%), compared with 83.7% for the All-Low rule. Where they disagreed with published labels, they were usually stricter: ARBITER in 88/124 cells and Unassisted in 69/115. ARBITER had greater sensitivity for Some concerns or High and lower specificity. Overall κ was 0.44 (0.32–0.56) and 0.42 (0.27–0.56), respectively; these ratings were not adjudicated. Confusion matrices, per-meta-analysis estimates, full agreement metrics, paired differences and post hoc unweighted agreement are in <supplement>; the meta-analysis forest is in <supplement>.

context: Adjudicators usually upheld stricter model ratings among cells with an agreed choice (Figure 4B). They agreed with stricter ARBITER ratings in 73/77 cells (94.8%; 95% CI 90.4–98.7) and stricter Unassisted ratings in 48/59 (81.4%; 73.2–89.4). For more lenient ratings, the corresponding counts were 22/28 (78.6%; 63.6–91.7) and 19/38 (50.0%; 34.4–65.8). Split decisions were excluded from these denominators. The counts were prespecified; their intervals were added post hoc. Full direction-of-disagreement outcomes and published-label agreement with the adjudicators’ agreed choice are in <supplement>.

context: ARBITER was preferred in most adjudicated cells where the arms disagreed: 54/62 (87.1%; 95% CI 79.0–94.3), compared with 7/62 for Unassisted and 1/62 for neither (Figure 5). ARBITER's share was 60/80 for Adjudicator 1, 64/80 for Adjudicator 2 and 54/80 when all splits counted against ARBITER. In post hoc severity strata, ARBITER was preferred in 44/45 cells where it was stricter than Unassisted and 10/17 where it was more lenient. Before seeing any label, the adjudicators' independent ratings agreed with ARBITER in 107/154 and 120/154 cells, versus 69/154 and 76/154 with Unassisted (Table 2). Post hoc paired differences were 24.7 (16.2–32.9) and 28.6 (19.8–37.4) percentage points. Between adjudicators, weighted κ was 0.59 for independent ratings and 0.69 for preferred ratings. Preference sensitivities, post hoc severity strata and full independent- and preferred-rating agreement metrics are in <supplement>.

context: Unassisted losses often hinged on an individual signalling answer. Among 47 eligible losing ratings, 29 had at least one question that alone changed the rating; the analysis-plan question (5.1) did so in 18 (Figure 6). Localisation eligibility, classes and question frequencies are in <supplement>; unresolved independent answers are in <supplement>, and exploratory signalling-answer agreement is in <supplement>. In the post hoc document description, 13 of these 18 had a supplied registry record, protocol or statistical analysis plan, but none of the Unassisted justifications mentioned such documents (<supplement>). Availability did not establish relevance, including the De Waal mismatch. In the post hoc rules-only recomputation, 3 of the original 62 arm disagreements changed to ARBITER's preferred rating and 59 were unchanged (<supplement>). These corrections created ties: Unassisted label-equality credit rose from 7 to 10, while ARBITER retained 54. Across the benchmark, recomputation reduced Unassisted agreement with published labels from 395 to 385 of 510 and with the agreed choice from 69 to 64 of 129.

context: Unassisted broke the RoB 2 domain rules in 65/509 evaluable ratings (12.8%; 95% CI 10.0–15.6): 26 contradicted their own answers and 39 skipped a required question (Table 3). One domain lacked both a rating and answers. ARBITER had zero domain rule breaks by design and no recorded overrides in 510 domains; every quotation was found in its content-hashed stored source. All 1538 required active answers cited evidence, all 1407 text-span records were source-linked, and all 14 image regions were page-linked. All 102 audit files passed the independent verifier. Both arms' Overall ratings followed the rules in 102/102 trials, including a permitted ARBITER escalation. These checks establish structural consistency and source occurrence, rather than semantic justification. The full consistency audit, skipped-question sensitivity, quotation syntax and Unassisted justification content are in <supplement>.

context: ARBITER combines features that prior systems developed separately (Table 4). RobotReviewer established the link between automated ratings and reviewable text.[8] ROBoto2 computes flowchart ratings and retains original responses and human edits; it is a substantive precursor.[10] Huang and Choi examined algorithm-derived judgements, while Liang added post hoc source-support evaluation.[14–16] Saadi's structured agent-based work concerns ROBINS-I; its description does not establish external tool calling.[17] CPGPrompt contributes the broader informatics pattern of formal guideline paths, although an LLM navigates its trees.[18] ARBITER's contribution is the assessed combination of software-controlled answer acceptance, source-bound quotations, an independently verifiable audit file and disputed-cell adjudication. Several prior matched comparisons also used identical underlying sources; input parity is not an exclusive contribution. Condensed evidence and quotation locations for the prior-work comparison are in <supplement>.
intended_captions: Evidence and quotation locations for the prior-work comparison

context: Evaluation conclusions depended strongly on the chosen reference. Against published labels, exact agreement numerically favoured Unassisted; against the supplementary composite reference, the same ratings yielded weighted κ of 0.94 for ARBITER and 0.69 for Unassisted (<supplement>). The post hoc partition shows why absolute values need caution: both arms matched all 356 cells that retained published labels, while agreement on the 129 agreed-choice cells was 116 for ARBITER and 69 for Unassisted. The composite excludes split decisions and assumes unaudited agreed cells are correct. It is optimistic in absolute terms, and the direction of bias in the paired difference is not guaranteed. Evaluations should report published-label agreement alongside an independent reference, rule conformance and evidence checks. More defensible risk-of-bias ratings could affect evidence certainty, but effects on certainty judgements or clinical recommendations were not measured.
